title: Chandipura Virus Death Toll Passes 80 as India Deploys National Response Team
excerpt: The largest Chandipura outbreak in two decades has killed at least 82 people, mostly children, prompting India to send a national emergency team to Gujarat as the monsoon season fuels sandfly transmission.
body:
• India's Chandipura virus outbreak has killed at least 82 people — predominantly children under 15 — and infected 245 with acute encephalitis syndrome, making it the largest Chandipura outbreak in two decades.
  • The World Health Organization has issued a Disease Outbreak News report, and India has deployed a National Joint Outbreak Response Team (NJORT) to Gujarat, the worst-affected state.
  • The virus is transmitted by sandflies, which thrive during the monsoon season, and carries a case fatality rate of approximately 33% among confirmed cases.
  • No vaccine or specific antiviral treatment exists; management is entirely supportive, and public health efforts focus on vector control and early detection.

An Outbreak That Has Grown Beyond Expectations

What began as a cluster of unexplained child deaths in Gujarat has become the largest Chandipura virus outbreak India has seen in over two decades. According to the World Health Organization's Disease Outbreak News report, at least 82 people have died and 245 cases of acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) linked to the virus have been recorded across multiple Indian states.

The vast majority of victims are children under 15. Chandipura virus, a member of the Rhabdoviridae family first identified in Maharashtra in 1965, has a particular affinity for pediatric patients, in whom it causes rapid-onset encephalitis — inflammation of the brain — that can progress from fever to seizures to coma within 24 to 48 hours.

India Deploys National Response Team

The scale of the outbreak has triggered one of India's most significant public health mobilizations in recent years. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has deployed a National Joint Outbreak Response Team (NJORT) to Gujarat, where the highest concentration of cases has been recorded. The NJORT includes epidemiologists, entomologists, virologists, and pediatric specialists tasked with containing transmission and improving clinical outcomes.

Gujarat's health infrastructure has come under strain. District hospitals in affected areas have set up dedicated AES treatment wards, and the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has expanded diagnostic capacity by sending RT-PCR testing kits to state laboratories. Before this outbreak, Chandipura testing was available only at a handful of national reference laboratories.

"The challenge with Chandipura is the speed of progression. A child can go from a mild fever to critical encephalitis in under 48 hours. Early presentation to a health facility is the single most important factor in survival."

— WHO Disease Outbreak News report

How the Virus Spreads

Chandipura virus is transmitted primarily by Phlebotomus sandflies — tiny, nocturnal insects that breed in organic debris, cattle dung, and cracks in mud walls. The monsoon season, which runs from June through September, creates ideal breeding conditions: warm temperatures, high humidity, and standing water.

Unlike mosquito-borne viruses such as dengue or chikungunya, Chandipura has no sustained human-to-human transmission. Each case requires a sandfly bite, which means vector control is the primary prevention strategy. Health authorities have launched intensive fogging and insecticide spraying campaigns in affected districts, along with public awareness drives urging families to use bed nets — particularly for young children — and to seal gaps in walls and floors where sandflies nest.

No Vaccine, No Treatment

There is currently no vaccine or antiviral treatment for Chandipura virus. Patient management is entirely supportive: intravenous fluids, anticonvulsants for seizures, mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, and intensive monitoring. The case fatality rate stands at approximately 33% among confirmed cases — a figure that likely understates the true mortality because many cases in rural areas go undiagnosed.

Previous outbreaks, including a major one in Andhra Pradesh in 2003 that killed over 180 children, similarly lacked targeted treatments. Research into Chandipura therapeutics and vaccines has been limited, in part because the virus causes sporadic, geographically contained outbreaks that attract less sustained research funding than globally prevalent pathogens.

What the Diaspora Should Know

For NRIs planning travel to India during the monsoon season — particularly to rural Gujarat, Rajasthan, or Maharashtra — the outbreak is a reminder to take sandfly precautions seriously. Insect repellents containing DEET, permethrin-treated clothing, and fine-mesh bed nets are the most effective personal protection measures. Parents traveling with young children should be especially vigilant, as the virus disproportionately affects those under 15. Any child who develops a sudden high fever during or shortly after travel to affected areas should receive immediate medical attention.
